subject: paediatrics
title: Pediatric Upper GI Obstruction: GERD, Pyloric Stenosis, and Intussusception

steps.tx: Incompetence of the lower oesophageal sphincter produces retrograde passage of gastric contents into the oesophagus. Uncomplicated physiological reflux is benign in young infants, whereas **gastro-oesophageal reflux disease** manifests with poor weight gain, haematemesis, recurrent aspiration pneumonia, and Sandifer syndrome marked by paroxysmal torticollis. Upright post-prandial positioning and thickened feedings control mild symptoms, reserving proton pump inhibitors for confirmed erosive oesophagitis.
steps.say: Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease causes failure to thrive and Sandifer syndrome with neck contortions. Position feeds upright and use proton pump inhibitors when esophagitis develops.

left.title: Physiological Infant Reflux (Spitting Up)
points: Normal growth velocity and thriving infant
Peaks at four months, resolves by one year

right.title: Pathological GERD Features
points: Refusal of feeds, irritability, and arching
Failure to thrive with poor caloric intake

steps.tx: Hypertrophy and hyperplasia of the circular muscular layer of the pylorus obstructs gastric outflow. Typically presenting between three and six weeks of age, **infantile hypertrophic pyloric stenosis** occurs predominantly in first-born male infants, exhibiting a strong genetic predisposition. The clinical hallmark is progressive, non-bilious projectile vomiting occurring immediately after feeds, accompanied by persistent hunger and severe dehydration.
steps.say: Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis strikes first-born infant boys at three to six weeks of age. Projectile non-bilious vomiting immediately after feeds is the classic presentation.

vis.alt: Anatomical cross section and ultrasound features of thickened circular muscle in hypertrophic pyloric stenosis.
vis.caption: Pyloric muscle hypertrophy narrowing the gastric outlet and elongating the pyloric channel. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Physical examination during calm post-vomiting states reveals pathognomonic diagnostic signs of gastric outlet obstruction. Careful palpation in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium identifies a firm, mobile, non-tender **pyloric olive mass**, representing the hypertrophied pylorus. Visible peristaltic waves passing from left to right across the epigastrium may be observed preceding bouts of projectile emesis.
steps.say: Palpating an olive-sized mass in the right epigastrium confirms pyloric stenosis. Visible gastric peristalsis rolls from left to right across the infant's upper abdomen.

rows: Firm mass in right upper quadrant

steps.tx: Protracted loss of hydrochloric acid through repetitive vomiting induces severe systemic metabolic derangements. Infants develop profound **hypochloraemic hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis** as gastric hydrogen and chloride ions are depleted. Renal compensation initially conserves sodium by exchanging potassium, followed by paradoxical aciduria when severe hypokalaemia forces renal distal tubules to excrete hydrogen ions despite systemic alkalosis.
steps.say: Repeated emesis of stomach acid causes hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis with paradoxical aciduria. Always correct dehydration and electrolytes before undertaking surgical repair.

left.title: Electrolyte Derangements in HPS
points: Serum potassium drops from renal wasting

right.title: Preoperative Resuscitation Rules
points: Never operate while infant is alkalotic
Infuse isotonic saline with potassium chloride

steps.tx: Invagination of a proximal bowel segment into an adjacent distal lumen causes acute intestinal obstruction. The most common cause of acute bowel obstruction in infants between five and ten months of age is **ileocolic intussusception**, where hypertrophied Peyer patches secondary to viral gastroenteritis act as the lead point. The condition presents with sudden severe colicky paroxysms, drawing up of legs, vomiting, and lethargy.
steps.say: Ileocolic intussusception is the most common cause of infant intestinal obstruction. Sudden severe abdominal colic causes the child to draw their knees up to the chest.

vis.alt: Ultrasound scan showing target sign and pseudokidney appearance in ileocolic intussusception.
vis.caption: Ultrasonographic cross-section demonstrating concentric rings of intussusceptum within intussuscipiens. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Somatic abdominal examination during quiescent interludes reveals pathognomonic physical signs of bowel invagination. Palpation identifies a smooth, sausage-shaped mass in the right hypochondrium, accompanied by an empty right iliac fossa known as the **Dance sign in intussusception**. High-frequency ultrasonography demonstrates a classic target or doughnut sign on transverse projection and a pseudokidney appearance on longitudinal views.
steps.say: Palpating an empty right lower quadrant represents the sign of Dance. Abdominal ultrasound shows a target or doughnut sign with one hundred percent diagnostic sensitivity.

rows: Empty right iliac fossa from invagination
Felt between severe paroxysms of pain

steps.tx: Progressive venous congestion and lymphatic obstruction compromise the blood supply of the telescoping bowel. Venous ischaemia causes mucosal sloughing mixed with blood and mucus, producing diagnostic **currant jelly stools** evacuated per rectum. As arterial compromise ensues, transmural bowel necrosis, gangrene, and intestinal perforation develop rapidly, converting a reducible intussusception into a surgical emergency.
steps.say: Venous congestion causes mucosal sloughing, producing red currant jelly stools with mucus and blood. Bowel necrosis and perforation develop quickly if obstruction is unrelieved.

left.title: Early Intussusception Features
points: Legs drawn up to abdomen with crying
Normal stools initially; child quiet between bouts
High success rate with non-operative enema

right.title: Late Ischaemic Manifestations
points: Passage of red currant jelly stools per rectum

steps.tx: Non-operative therapeutic reduction represents the first-line intervention in the absence of peritonitis or shock. Under fluoroscopic or ultrasound monitoring, **pneumatic or hydrostatic reduction** is performed using air insufflation or isotonic saline enemas, exerting controlled retrograde intraluminal pressure. If reduction fails after three attempts, or if pneumoperitoneum or bowel strangulation is suspected, immediate operative laparotomy and manual reduction are indicated.
steps.say: Pneumatic air reduction under ultrasound guidance is the first-line therapy for early intussusception. Bowel perforation or peritonitis demands immediate open surgical reduction.

rows: Warm saline hung 1 metre above bed
Common in children older than 2 years
Requires surgical resection of bowel segment
